## interpolants.kt { #interpolants-kt }

[`smoothTo`](math.md#interpolants-kt--smoothto) wraps a target-producing lambda so that reading it eases toward the target instead
of jumping to it.

The returned [`Interpolant`](math.md#interpolants-kt-interpolant) is also a `HasUniform`/`ProgressingUniform`, so it can sit
where Field expects a uniform and be re-evaluated per frame. It implements
[`NeedsStartingValue`](math.md#interpolants-kt-needsstartingvalue), and whoever binds it is responsible for calling `startAt` with the
current value — until that happens the interpolant simply reports the target and marks itself
complete.

Interpolation is linear and only covers `Float`, `Double`, `Int`, `Long` and
`Vector2f`/`Vector3f`/`Vector4f`; any other type completes immediately at the target. Progress
is either time-based (`time` seconds), a fixed number of evaluations (`steps`, default 100), or
frame-based by supplying `clock = frameClock(fps) { frameNumber }`. Time-based interpolation uses
`System.nanoTime` by default; an injected clock makes offline and fixed-rate rendering independent
of scheduler pauses. The interpolation is one-shot: once it reaches the target it stays there.

[`inertialTo`](math.md#interpolants-kt--inertialto) is the other half of the library, for the case [`smoothTo`](math.md#interpolants-kt--smoothto) handles badly: a target that
keeps moving. It takes the same `time`/`steps`/`clock` arguments, but eases on a smoothstep whose
timing it re-solves whenever the target changes, so a re-aim carries the velocity it already had
instead of restarting from a standstill.

## spectral.kt { #spectral-kt }

Frequency-domain / spectral analysis family for the stdlib DSP toolkit.

This is the frequency-domain companion to `timeseries.kt` (which is entirely time-domain): a
pure-Kotlin FFT, analysis windows, a [`Spectrum`](math.md#spectral-kt-spectrum) and a [`Spectrogram`](math.md#spectral-kt-spectrogram) (STFT), classic spectral
features (centroid / spread / rolloff / flux / flatness / RMS / energy), and streaming
[`FloatFilter`](math.md#timeseries-kt-floatfilter) wrappers so those features drop straight into the time-domain filter chain in
`timeseries.kt` (compose with `then`).

Everything is plain `Double`/`Float` math — no external DSP dependency — so it works headless in
a box, a test, or a docs capture. The FFT is an iterative Cooley–Tukey radix-2 core with a
Bluestein (chirp-z) fallback so arbitrary (non-power-of-two) lengths transform exactly.

### WindowType { #spectral-kt-windowtype }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">enum</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">WindowType</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/analysis/spectral/#L286)

Which analysis window to taper a frame with before transforming it — the trade between how sharply you can separate two nearby frequencies and how much a strong one smears into its neighbours.

Constants: `RECTANGULAR`, `HANN`, `HAMMING`, `BLACKMAN`.

| <a id="spectral-kt--windows--hamming"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">hamming</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">n</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">periodic</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">false</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/analysis/spectral/#L326) | `0.54 - 0.46·cos(2πi/d)` — like [`hann`](math.md#spectral-kt--windows--hann) but it does **not** reach zero at the ends, which is what buys its slightly better resolution and slightly worse far-field leakage. |
| <a id="spectral-kt--windows--blackman"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">blackman</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">n</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">periodic</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">false</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/analysis/spectral/#L337) | The three-term `0.42 - 0.5·cos(w) + 0.08·cos(2w)` window: the strongest leakage suppression here, and the widest main lobe — about 1.5 times [`hann`](math.md#spectral-kt--windows--hann)'s null-to-null width, so two frequencies Hann would just separate blur into one here. |
| <a id="spectral-kt--windows--coherentgain"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">coherentGain</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">window</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/analysis/spectral/#L347) | Coherent gain (mean) of a window — used to compensate amplitude when a window is applied. |

### Spectrogram { #spectral-kt-spectrogram }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">Spectrogram</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">framesRe</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Array</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">framesIm</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Array</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">sampleRate</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">fftSize</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">hopSize</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">window</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">WindowType</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/audio/analysis/spectral/#L472)

## linalg_mesh.kt { #linalg-mesh-kt }

The short vector aliases ([`Vec2`](math.md#linalg-kt-vec2), [`Vec3`](math.md#linalg-kt-vec3), [`Vec4`](math.md#linalg-kt-vec4), [`Quat`](math.md#linalg-kt-quat), [`DualQuat`](math.md#linalg-kt-dualquat)) plus the constructors and
point-cloud helpers that sit on top of Field's generated `afield.math.linalg` types.

`vec(...)` is the usual way to make one — from numbers, by copying, or by concatenating a
scalar with a smaller vector — and `quat` / `dualquat` do the same for rotations. Collections
of vectors gain `center`, `median` / `medianVec` and `aabbBounds` in 2D, 3D and 4D; 3D also
gets `obbBounds` (a box aligned to the covariance matrix's principal axes, found by power
iteration, so a PCA fit rather than a minimal-volume one),
`convexHull`, which goes through the QuickHull3D library and returns the input unchanged if the
hull cannot be built, and `convexHullPeelingMedian`, which peels hulls away and returns the
centre of what is left — a single point, not a cloud. [`Cuboid`](math.md#linalg-spatial-kt-cuboid) is a separate plain 3D
box-with-size type used for layout-style union / inset / intersects work.

These vector types are mutable and most operations mutate the receiver, so copy first
(`Vec3(existing)`) when you need to keep the original. Swizzles and the *vector* `invoke`, `%=`
and `len` operators are absent here: they are generated for every float vector into
`Swizzles.kt` and `VectorOperators.kt` by `tools/linalg-generator`. `%=` for [`Quat`](math.md#linalg-kt-quat) and
[`DualQuat`](math.md#linalg-kt-dualquat) is defined here, because no generator emits those.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/mesh/linalg_mesh.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/mesh/linalg_mesh/)

## CubicBezier3D.kt { #cubicbezier3d-kt }

A double-precision 3D cubic Bézier for planning paths with a minimum turning radius.

[`CubicBezier3D`](math.md#cubicbezier3d-kt-cubicbezier3d) evaluates positions and tangents, gives a conservative lower bound on the
curve's radius with [`CubicBezier3D.minimumRadiusBound`](math.md#cubicbezier3d-kt--cubicbezier3d--minimumradiusbound), and turns the curve into a polyline
within a caller-chosen deviation with [`CubicBezier3D.flatten`](math.md#cubicbezier3d-kt--cubicbezier3d--flatten). Degenerate curves, cusps and
invalid requests throw rather than return a guess. `CubicBezier3DTest` covers these cases,
including invariance under translation, rotation and change of units.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/path/planning/CubicBezier3D.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/path/planning/CubicBezier3D/)

## Point3D.kt { #point3d-kt }

A small immutable 3D point type used by the path-planning curves in this package.

[`Point3D`](math.md#point3d-kt-point3d) carries finite double coordinates with the vector operations a curve needs:
addition, difference, scaling, [`Point3D.dot`](math.md#point3d-kt--point3d--dot), [`Point3D.cross`](math.md#point3d-kt--point3d--cross), [`Point3D.length`](math.md#point3d-kt--point3d--length) and
[`Point3D.normalized`](math.md#point3d-kt--point3d--normalized).
[`CubicBezier3D`](math.md#cubicbezier3d-kt-cubicbezier3d) is built from it.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/path/planning/Point3D.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/path/planning/Point3D/)

## linalg_spatial.kt { #linalg-spatial-kt }

The short vector aliases ([`Vec2`](math.md#linalg-kt-vec2), [`Vec3`](math.md#linalg-kt-vec3), [`Vec4`](math.md#linalg-kt-vec4), [`Quat`](math.md#linalg-kt-quat), [`DualQuat`](math.md#linalg-kt-dualquat)) plus the constructors and
point-cloud helpers that sit on top of Field's generated `afield.math.linalg` types.

`vec(...)` is the usual way to make one — from numbers, by copying, or by concatenating a
scalar with a smaller vector — and `quat` / `dualquat` do the same for rotations. Collections
of vectors gain `center`, `median` / `medianVec` and `aabbBounds` in 2D, 3D and 4D; 3D also
gets `obbBounds` (a box aligned to the covariance matrix's principal axes, found by power
iteration, so a PCA fit rather than a minimal-volume one),
`convexHull`, which goes through the QuickHull3D library and returns the input unchanged if the
hull cannot be built, and `convexHullPeelingMedian`, which peels hulls away and returns the
centre of what is left — a single point, not a cloud. [`Cuboid`](math.md#linalg-spatial-kt-cuboid) is a separate plain 3D
box-with-size type used for layout-style union / inset / intersects work.

These vector types are mutable and most operations mutate the receiver, so copy first
(`Vec3(existing)`) when you need to keep the original. Swizzles and the *vector* `invoke`, `%=`
and `len` operators are absent here: they are generated for every float vector into
`Swizzles.kt` and `VectorOperators.kt` by `tools/linalg-generator`. `%=` for [`Quat`](math.md#linalg-kt-quat) and
[`DualQuat`](math.md#linalg-kt-dualquat) is defined here, because no generator emits those.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/geometry/spatial/linalg_spatial.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/geometry/spatial/linalg_spatial/)

## autodiff.kt { #autodiff-kt }

Reverse-mode automatic differentiation over `Double` scalars — exact gradients for ordinary
Kotlin arithmetic, in one pass, whatever the expression's size.

The alternative is a numerical gradient, which is the default in [`fitGradient`](function.md#functionfit-kt--fitgradient) and
[`leastSquares`](math.md#leastsquares-kt--leastsquares): central differences over the loss or the residuals, `2·n` extra evaluations per
step, and a truncation-against-round-off compromise you tune with an `fdStep`. Reverse mode
costs one forward pass plus one backward sweep for *all* `n` derivatives, and the answer is
exact to the last few ulps.

### AD and the tape

[`AD`](math.md#autodiff-kt-ad) is a scalar that remembers how it was made. Arithmetic on [`AD`](math.md#autodiff-kt-ad) values appends to an [`ADTape`](math.md#autodiff-kt-adtape)
— a flat array of (value, up-to-two parents, up-to-two local partials) — so
`(a * b + sin(c)) / 2.0` reads exactly like `Double` arithmetic and records a graph as it goes. The
backward sweep walks that array once in reverse accumulating adjoints. Because every node has at
most two parents, the tape is five parallel arrays of primitives — value, two parent indices,
two partials — and there is no object churn beyond the [`AD`](math.md#autodiff-kt-ad) handles themselves.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val g = grad { p -> (p[0] - 3.0).sq() + 2.0 * (p[1] + 1.0).sq() }
g(doubleArrayOf(0.0, 0.0))          // [-6.0, 4.0], exact

val (v, d) = valueAndDerivative(0.4) { x -> exp(-x * x) * sin(6.0 * x) }
```

[`grad`](math.md#autodiff-kt--grad) returns a *function*, so it composes with the optimizers in `autodiff_optimize.kt`
([`minimize`](math.md#autodiff-optimize-kt--minimize), [`adam`](math.md#autodiff-optimize-kt--adam), [`sgd`](math.md#autodiff-optimize-kt--sgd), [`lbfgs`](math.md#autodiff-optimize-kt--lbfgs)) without a wrapper. [`gradAt`](math.md#autodiff-kt--gradat), [`valueAndGrad`](math.md#autodiff-kt--valueandgrad), [`jacobian`](math.md#autodiff-kt--jacobian) and
[`hessian`](math.md#autodiff-kt--hessian) are the immediate forms.

### Forward mode

[`Dual2`](math.md#autodiff-forward-kt-dual2) is a second-order forward-mode number (value, first derivative, second derivative along a
direction). It is the right tool when there is one input and many outputs — the reverse of
reverse mode — and it is what makes [`hessian`](math.md#autodiff-kt--hessian) *exact* rather than a finite difference of an exact
gradient: `vᵀHv` falls out of a single [`Dual2`](math.md#autodiff-forward-kt-dual2) pass, and polarisation recovers the off-diagonal
entries. See [`directionalDerivative`](math.md#autodiff-forward-kt--directionalderivative) and [`secondDerivative`](math.md#autodiff-forward-kt--secondderivative).

### The kink convention

`abs`, `min`, `max` and `relu` are not differentiable at their kink, so a convention has to be
chosen. This library **splits the derivative evenly at an exact tie**: `min(a, b)` with `a == b`
sends 0.5 to each argument, and `relu` (which is `max(x, 0)`) has derivative 0.5 at zero. That is
what a central difference reports at a kink, so the analytic gradient and the finite-difference
oracle agree there too, and it makes `abs(x)` and `max(x, -x)` agree on derivative 0 at zero,
which is the minimum-norm subgradient. PyTorch instead defines `relu'(0) = 0`.

### What is not covered

- **Mutation.** [`AD`](math.md#autodiff-kt-ad) is immutable. `x += y` on a `var` rebinds it to a fresh handle and appends
  a node; the handle it replaced stays valid, and an accumulation loop therefore grows the tape
  by one node per iteration.
- **Control flow** is differentiated *as taken*: an `if (x > 0.0)` records only the branch that
  ran, which is the correct derivative of the piecewise function everywhere except at the
  switch-over. Comparisons on [`AD`](math.md#autodiff-kt-ad) therefore return plain `Boolean` and carry no derivative.
- **Piecewise-constant ops** (`floor`, `round`, `sign`, `quantize`) have derivative 0 by
  definition, and no finite-difference oracle exists at their jumps.
- **Third and higher derivatives** are not available. [`hessian`](math.md#autodiff-kt--hessian) is exact; a third-order term
  would need a `Dual3` or a nestable tape and neither is here.
- **Tape size** grows with the number of *operations executed*, not with `n`. A loss over 100k
  samples builds a 100k-node tape per evaluation; that is the memory cost of reverse mode and it
  is not chunked or checkpointed.

At an exact tie the derivative splits 0.5/0.5 — see the kink convention in the file KDoc. |

### ADTape { #autodiff-kt-adtape }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">ADTape</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/math/autodiff/autodiff/#L125)

The append-only record of every operation performed on the [`AD`](math.md#autodiff-kt-ad) values that belong to it.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <a id="autodiff-kt--adtape--size"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">size</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/math/autodiff/autodiff/#L135) | The number of operations recorded so far — the tape's length, useful for budgeting. |
| <a id="autodiff-kt--adtape--variable"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">variable</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">value</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">AD</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/math/autodiff/autodiff/#L167) | A tracked scalar holding `value` with no parents — a leaf of the tape. |
| <a id="autodiff-kt--adtape--constant"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">constant</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">value</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">AD</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/math/autodiff/autodiff/#L173) | A tracked scalar holding `value` that is treated as a leaf — identical in mechanics to [`variable`](math.md#autodiff-kt--adtape--variable), named differently to say "I do not intend to differentiate this". |
| <a id="autodiff-kt--adtape--variables"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">variables</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">values</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">AD</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/math/autodiff/autodiff/#L176) | [`variable`](math.md#autodiff-kt--adtape--variable) for a whole vector, in order — the usual way to start a gradient. |
| <a id="autodiff-kt--adtape--backward"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">backward</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">output</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">AD</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/math/autodiff/autodiff/#L186) | Sweeps backwards from `output`, returning the adjoint (∂output/∂node) of **every** node on the tape, indexed by `AD.index`. |

### AD { #autodiff-kt-ad }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">AD</span> <span class="k">internal</span> <span class="k">constructor</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">tape</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">ADTape</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">internal</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">index</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Comparable</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">AD</span><span class="p">&gt;</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/math/autodiff/autodiff/#L214)

A scalar that remembers how it was computed: a value plus its position on an [`ADTape`](math.md#autodiff-kt-adtape).

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <a id="autodiff-kt--ad--tape"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">tape</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">ADTape</span></code> | The tape this value was recorded on. Two [`AD`](math.md#autodiff-kt-ad)s can only be combined if they share one. |
| <a id="autodiff-kt--ad--value"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="k">value</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/math/autodiff/autodiff/#L221) | The plain numeric value, with no derivative information. |

## autodiff_forward.kt { #autodiff-forward-kt }

Forward-mode automatic differentiation to **second order** — the other half of `autodiff.kt`.

A [`Dual2`](math.md#autodiff-forward-kt-dual2) is a truncated Taylor series `(v, v', v'')` carried along a single direction. Every
operation propagates all three components, so one evaluation of an expression in [`Dual2`](math.md#autodiff-forward-kt-dual2)
arithmetic returns the value, the directional first derivative and the directional *curvature* at
once — no tape, no backward sweep, and no allocation beyond one three-`Double` object per node.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val t = taylor2(0.6) { x -> exp(-x * x) * sin(6.0 * x) }
t.value; t.first; t.second      // f, f', f'' at 0.6, all exact
```

### Forward or reverse

Reverse mode ([`grad`](math.md#autodiff-kt--grad)) wins when there are many inputs and one output — a loss over a parameter
vector. Forward mode wins in the opposite shape (one input, many outputs: a parametric curve and
every quantity derived from it), and it is the only one of the two that reaches second order.
[`hessian`](math.md#autodiff-kt--hessian) in `autodiff.kt` is built on this file: `vᵀHv` is exactly [`Dual2.second`](math.md#autodiff-forward-kt--dual2--second) after a pass
seeded along `v`.

The op vocabulary mirrors `autodiff.kt` name for name — [`sin`](math.md#autodiff-forward-kt--sin), [`exp`](math.md#autodiff-forward-kt--exp), [`tanh`](math.md#autodiff-forward-kt--tanh), [`max`](math.md#autodiff-forward-kt--max),
[`pow`](math.md#autodiff-forward-kt--pow) and friends are overloaded on both [`AD`](math.md#autodiff-kt-ad) and [`Dual2`](math.md#autodiff-forward-kt-dual2), so the *same* expression body can be
written once against a shape and evaluated either way (see [`ADFunction2`](math.md#autodiff-forward-kt-adfunction2)).

### Conventions and gaps

- The kink convention matches `autodiff.kt`: [`max`](math.md#autodiff-forward-kt--max) / [`min`](math.md#autodiff-forward-kt--min) split evenly at an exact tie, so
  `relu''` is 0 everywhere and `relu'(0)` is 0.5.
- [`pow`](math.md#autodiff-forward-kt--pow) with a *tracked* exponent is evaluated as `exp(b · ln a)` and therefore requires a
  strictly positive base; the constant-exponent [`Dual2.pow`](math.md#autodiff-forward-kt--dual2--pow) has no such restriction.
- Third and higher derivatives are not represented. A `Dual3` would be a mechanical extension of
  the same chain rule; it is not here.

### ADFunction2 { #autodiff-forward-kt-adfunction2 }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">typealias</span> <span class="nc">ADFunction2</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="p">(</span><span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">Dual2</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="nc">Dual2</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/math/autodiff/autodiff_forward/#L388)

A scalar function of a vector written once against [`Dual2`](math.md#autodiff-forward-kt-dual2), so it can be handed to both [`hessian`](math.md#autodiff-kt--hessian) and [`directionalDerivative`](math.md#autodiff-forward-kt--directionalderivative) without being restated.

## autodiff_geometry.kt { #autodiff-geometry-kt }

Differentiable geometry: tracked vectors, planar inverse kinematics on an [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline) chain, and a
differentiable circle packing — the part of the AD layer whose results are drawable.

[`ADVec2`](math.md#autodiff-geometry-kt-advec2) and [`ADVec3`](math.md#autodiff-geometry-kt-advec3) are pairs and triples of [`AD`](math.md#autodiff-kt-ad). They convert to and from Field's own
[`Vec2`](math.md#linalg-kt-vec2) / [`Vec3`](math.md#linalg-kt-vec3) (the generated, *mutable*, float-backed `Vector2f` / `Vector3f`), and every
operation on them is expressed in the same scalar ops as the rest of `autodiff.kt`. There are no
vector-specific derivative rules here; the point is that `(joint - target).length()` reads as
itself inside a loss instead of as unrolled components.

### Inverse kinematics

[`solveIk`](math.md#autodiff-geometry-kt--solveik) finds the joint angles of a planar chain of fixed-length links by minimising
`|endEffector - target|²` with exact gradients. Forward kinematics is a cumulative sum of angles
and a running position — differentiable throughout — so L-BFGS reaches a sub-micron reach in tens
of iterations, and the result is an [`FLine`](graphics.md#fline-kt-fline) you can draw.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val chain = IkChain(vec(120f, 300f), doubleArrayOf(90.0, 80.0, 70.0, 55.0))
val solved = solveIk(chain, vec(360f, 150f))
showPlane(listOf(chain.toFLine(solved.angles)))
```

A pure reach objective is under-determined for more than two links, so [`IkOptions.smoothness`](math.md#autodiff-geometry-kt--ikoptions--smoothness)
offers a curvature penalty between consecutive links. It is off by default, and it is a trade
rather than a free regulariser: the two terms compete, so a positive smoothness buys a straighter
pose and charges reach accuracy for it. The charge is small out in the open and large near the
base, where reaching at all needs tight folds. On the four-link chain in the example above,
`AutoDiffGeometryTest` pins a target 216 units away as exact to under a thousandth of a unit
with no penalty and inside 12 units under a heavy one; a target close to the anchor is exact
without the penalty and more than a unit short at `smoothness = 0.02`.
[`IkSolution.reachError`](math.md#autodiff-geometry-kt--iksolution--reacherror) reports the shortfall either way, so a solve that traded accuracy away
can be told from one that converged.

### Packing

[`packCircles`](math.md#autodiff-geometry-kt--packcircles) minimises pairwise overlap and wall penetration under a gentle pull toward the
centre. Every term is a `relu(...)²` hinge, which is exactly where the even-split kink convention
in `autodiff.kt` matters: at the moment two circles touch, the penalty's gradient is *half* what a
naive one-sided rule would give, and the packing settles rather than chattering.

## autodiff_optimize.kt { #autodiff-optimize-kt }

Gradient-descent optimizers that consume the exact gradients from `autodiff.kt` — [`sgd`](math.md#autodiff-optimize-kt--sgd), [`adam`](math.md#autodiff-optimize-kt--adam)
and [`lbfgs`](math.md#autodiff-optimize-kt--lbfgs), behind one [`minimize`](math.md#autodiff-optimize-kt--minimize) front door.

All three are **deterministic given their seed** and all three record a full [`OptimizeRun.losses`](math.md#autodiff-optimize-kt--optimizerun--losses)
trajectory which you can hand straight to `showSignals("loss" to run.losses)` and look at.
[`FnEvolveRun`](function.md#functionevolve-kt-fnevolverun) and [`FnFitRun`](function.md#functionfit-kt-fnfitrun) carry a `losses` list of the same shape, so a fit, an evolve and an
optimisation all replay and plot the same way.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val run = minimize(doubleArrayOf(-1.2, 1.0), OptimizeOptions(method = OptimizeMethod.LBFGS)) { p ->
    (1.0 - p[0]).sq() + 100.0 * (p[1] - p[0].sq()).sq()   // Rosenbrock
}
run.x          // ~[1, 1]
run.losses     // the trajectory, ready to plot
```

### Which one

- [`lbfgs`](math.md#autodiff-optimize-kt--lbfgs) is the right default for a smooth deterministic objective with a handful to a few
  hundred parameters: it builds a curvature model from the last `m` steps and takes
  Newton-shaped strides, so it reaches machine-precision minima in tens of iterations where Adam
  is still crawling. It needs the objective to actually be smooth; a kinked or noisy loss will
  make its line search flail.
- [`adam`](math.md#autodiff-optimize-kt--adam) is the robust workhorse for a rough, kinked or stochastic landscape, and the one that
  tolerates a badly scaled parameter vector without preconditioning.
- [`sgd`](math.md#autodiff-optimize-kt--sgd) with momentum is here because it is sometimes what you want *artistically* — a slower,
  visibly settling trajectory with a tunable inertia, which reads as motion rather than as a
  solver converging.

The line search inside [`lbfgs`](math.md#autodiff-optimize-kt--lbfgs) is backtracking Armijo, which guarantees monotone descent but not
the curvature (Wolfe) condition; the L-BFGS memory therefore skips any update pair with
non-positive curvature rather than letting an indefinite model through.

| <a id="autodiff-optimize-kt--optimizerun--options"></a><code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">options</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">OptimizeOptions</span></code> | The options this run was made with. |

| <a id="autodiff-optimize-kt--optimizerun--gradientinfnorm"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">gradientInfNorm</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/math/autodiff/autodiff_optimize/#L216) | The gradient's infinity norm at [`x`](math.md#autodiff-optimize-kt--optimizerun--x). |
| <a id="autodiff-optimize-kt--optimizerun--equals"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">override</span> <span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">equals</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">other</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Any</span><span class="o">?</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/math/autodiff/autodiff_optimize/#L225) | Two runs are equal when [`x`](math.md#autodiff-optimize-kt--optimizerun--x), `value`, [`losses`](math.md#autodiff-optimize-kt--optimizerun--losses), `iterations`, [`evaluations`](math.md#autodiff-optimize-kt--optimizerun--evaluations), [`converged`](math.md#autodiff-optimize-kt--optimizerun--converged), [`reason`](math.md#autodiff-optimize-kt--optimizerun--reason) and [`options`](math.md#autodiff-optimize-kt--optimizerun--options) all match. [`trajectory`](math.md#autodiff-optimize-kt--optimizerun--trajectory) is left out: it is a `List<DoubleArray>` and `DoubleArray.equals` is identity, so including it would make any two separately-computed runs unequal whatever their contents. It is fully determined by [`initialX`](math.md#autodiff-optimize-kt--optimizerun--initialx), [`options`](math.md#autodiff-optimize-kt--optimizerun--options) and the objective, and [`x`](math.md#autodiff-optimize-kt--optimizerun--x) and [`losses`](math.md#autodiff-optimize-kt--optimizerun--losses) compare its endpoint and its whole value trace. |

## pf.kt { #pf-kt }

An unscented Kalman filter, and a particle filter whose particles each carry one.

[`UnscentedKalmanFilter`](math.md#pf-kt-unscentedkalmanfilter) keeps a mean and covariance and takes the transition and observation
models as lambdas; [`UnscentedKalmanFilter.updateWithLikelihood`](math.md#pf-kt--unscentedkalmanfilter--updatewithlikelihood) returns the log measurement
likelihood, which is exactly what [`UKFParticleFilter`](math.md#pf-kt-ukfparticlefilter) accumulates into each particle's log
weight. A [`UKFParticle`](math.md#pf-kt-ukfparticle) holds a UKF for the continuous state plus a hypothesis of your own
type `H` for the discrete or non-Gaussian part. [`UKFParticleFilter.resampleIfNeeded`](math.md#pf-kt--ukfparticlefilter--resampleifneeded) does
systematic resampling once the effective sample size drops below a fraction of the particle
count, and can immediately roughen the resampled means ([`RougheningOptions`](math.md#pf-kt-rougheningoptions)) so exact clones
separate again.

State and measurement dimensions are restricted to 1..3 — the private determinant helper only
covers those sizes and everything `require`s it. The linear algebra (`Matrix` is just
`Array<DoubleArray>`; Cholesky with escalating jitter, Gauss–Jordan inverse) is private to this
file, has no external dependency, and allocates fresh arrays on every step.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/math/estimation/pf.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/math/estimation/pf/)

**Used in:** [State estimation: tracking what you cannot measure](../state_estimation_examples.md)

| <a id="pf-kt--ukfparticlefilter--resamplesystematic"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">resampleSystematic</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">random</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Random</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Random</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">Default</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">roughening</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">RougheningOptions</span><span class="o">?</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">null</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/math/estimation/pf/#L593) | Resamples unconditionally by systematic resampling: one uniform draw, then `n` evenly spaced strides through the cumulative weights, so a particle with weight `w` gets about `n·w` copies. |
| <a id="pf-kt--ukfparticlefilter--roughenstatemeans"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">roughenStateMeans</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">options</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">RougheningOptions</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">RougheningOptions</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">random</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Random</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">Random</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="nc">Default</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/math/estimation/pf/#L645) | Roughens only the continuous UKF means. This is useful immediately after resampling, when many particles may be exact clones. |

SIMD helpers for dense `DoubleArray` arithmetic, using the JDK Vector API: [`DenseDoubleOps`](math.md#densedoubleops-kt-densedoubleops)
provides `dot`, `combine` and `scale`.

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">object</span> <span class="nc">DenseDoubleOps</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/math/functions/DenseDoubleOps/#L45)

Allocation-free SIMD operations on equal-length dense double arrays, with scalar tails. Reductions use lane-wise accumulation, so last-bit rounding can differ from a scalar sum. Destination arrays may alias either input for elementwise operations.

## Functions.kt { #functions-kt }

The `Fn` toolkit: one-dimensional signals as values you can build, compose, sample and draw.

Nearly everything lives inside the [`Functions`](math.md#functions-kt-functions) object, and most of it as extension functions,
so callers normally work inside `with(Functions) { ... }`. A `Functions.Fn` is an evaluator
plus the `Functions.Domain` it is meant to be sampled over (default `0.0..1.0`). Sources —
`sin`, `saw`, `triangle`, `square`, the `pulseTrain` / `pulseBurst` family, the noise and
`fbm` generators, and keyframe interpolants such as `catmullRomSpline` and `monotoneCubic` —
combine through arithmetic operators, through chainable `Fn` extensions (`stretch`, `repeat`,
`fold`, `quantize`, `echo`, `convolve`, `blur`, ...), and through reusable `FnTransform`
pipelines applied with `/`. Arrangement in time is `timeline { }` and the `List<Fn>`
combinators (`sequence`, `randomPermute`, `morph`, `stack`, `average`); those rearrange `Fn`s
and timeline chunks and hand the result back to the same evaluator rather than introducing a
second one.

Every combinator also records an `FnGraphNode` recipe alongside the closure (see
`FunctionGraph.kt`), which is what makes graphs inspectable and rewritable rather than opaque
lambdas. On the output side: `toDoubleArray` and the `sample*` helpers for numbers, `toFLine`
for drawing, `plotHtml` for a self-contained plot, and `Fn.plot`, which displays into the
active `Box` and throws when there is none (`Box.plot` takes the `Fn` explicitly instead).

[`RbfKernel`](math.md#functions-kt-rbfkernel), [`RbfKernels`](math.md#functions-kt-rbfkernels) and [`RbfInterpolator`](math.md#functions-kt-rbfinterpolator) at the top of the file are the scattered-data
fitter behind `Functions.rbf`; it solves a dense n×n system per construction, so it is sized
for handfuls of control points, not thousands.
Its counterpart in two or more dimensions, [`RbfField`](math.md#rbffield-kt-rbffield) in `RbfField.kt`, fits a surface through
values at scattered points with the same kernels.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/math/functions/Functions.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/math/functions/Functions/)

**Used in:** [Functions to FLine examples (Field graphics)](../functions_examples.md)

Zero gives negative infinity and negative values NaN. |

## PatternRewriteSmokeTest.kt { #patternrewritesmoketest-kt }

Smoke for the pattern-rewrite layer ([`PatternRewrite`](workspace.md#patternrewrite-kt-patternrewrite)), a structural source-to-source rewriter
that lets a box author its own `rewrite { ... }` rules on top of the PSI macro pass.

Most cases are black-box: they feed a source string (rule plus code) through
[`PatternRewrite.expand`](workspace.md#patternrewrite-kt--patternrewrite--expand) with the standalone [`FieldKtParser`](workspace.md#fieldktparser-kt-fieldktparser) as the PSI environment and assert on
the emitted text, with no REPL. The unquote and fragment-rule cases drive a real
[`KotlinInterface2`](workspace.md#kotlininterface2-kt-kotlininterface2) through `applyMacros`. The cases cover match and no-match, non-linearity,
paren-modulo, the precedence hazard, the quote barrier, first-match-wins declaration order,
guards, variadic holes, unquote, ambient and local rules, and termination of a non-converging
rule.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/math/functions/PatternRewriteSmokeTest.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/math/functions/PatternRewriteSmokeTest/)

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">RbfField</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">dimension</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">kernel</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">RbfKernel</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="nc">RbfKernels</span><span class="p">.</span><span class="n">thinPlate</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">smoothing</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">0.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">trend</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Boolean</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">true</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/math/functions/RbfField/#L33)

Radial basis function interpolation in two or more dimensions: a smooth surface through values scattered at points in a plane, or a volume, with no grid. The 1D version, [`RbfInterpolator`](math.md#functions-kt-rbfinterpolator) behind `Functions.rbf`, fits a curve through `(x, y)` samples; this one fits `f(point)` through `(point, value)` samples, with the same [`RbfKernel`](math.md#functions-kt-rbfkernel)s.

## math.kt { #math-kt }

`Number`-taking overloads of the trigonometric functions, so `sin(1)` and `sin(1f)` work
without writing `.toDouble()` at every call site.

Covers the circular functions and their inverses ([`sin`](math.md#math-kt--sin), [`cos`](math.md#math-kt--cos), [`tan`](math.md#math-kt--tan), [`asin`](math.md#math-kt--asin), [`acos`](math.md#math-kt--acos), [`atan`](math.md#math-kt--atan),
[`atan2`](math.md#math-kt--atan2)) and the hyperbolic ones ([`sinh`](math.md#math-kt--sinh), [`cosh`](math.md#math-kt--cosh), [`tanh`](math.md#math-kt--tanh), [`asinh`](math.md#math-kt--asinh), [`acosh`](math.md#math-kt--acosh), [`atanh`](math.md#math-kt--atanh)). Each is a
one-line delegate to the matching `kotlin.math` function and always returns `Double`.

## GaussianProcess.kt { #gaussianprocess-kt }

Exact Gaussian-process regression: fit scalar observations (values and, optionally, slopes) and query the posterior mean, variance and joint covariance.

[`GaussianProcess`](math.md#gaussianprocess-kt-gaussianprocess) factors the training covariance once and reuses that Cholesky factor for every
prediction. [`GpPrediction`](math.md#gaussianprocess-kt-gpprediction) is a single mean and variance with an [interval](math.md#gaussianprocess-kt--gpprediction--interval);
[`GpFunctional`](math.md#gaussianprocess-kt-gpfunctional) names a value or a derivative to query jointly; [`GpDerivativeObservation`](math.md#gaussianprocess-kt-gpderivativeobservation) trains on a
measured slope. [`GpNumerics`](math.md#gaussianprocess-kt-gpnumerics) holds the jitter and size limits, and the jitter actually used is
reported back as `jitterUsed`. `logMarginalLikelihood` is the evidence that the fitters in
`GpFit.kt` maximise.

### GaussianProcess { #gaussianprocess-kt-gaussianprocess }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">GaussianProcess</span> <span class="k">private</span> <span class="k">constructor</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">dimensions</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">kernel</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">GpKernel</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">private</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">priorMean</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="p">(</span><span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">)</span> <span class="o">-&gt;</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">private</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Array</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">private</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">axes</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">IntArray</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">private</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">y</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">private</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">noise</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">numerics</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">GpNumerics</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/math/gp/GaussianProcess/#L98)

Exact dense GP regression in any finite input dimension, with 1D/2D/3D conveniences below. Fit once; the training Cholesky is reused by predictions. No matrix inverse is formed. Samples come from [`posterior`](math.md#gaussianprocess-kt--gaussianprocess--posterior), whose full covariance retains correlations between queries. Training data may include slopes ([`GpDerivativeObservation`](math.md#gaussianprocess-kt-gpderivativeobservation)); values and slopes can be queried jointly ([`posterior`](math.md#gaussianprocess-kt--gaussianprocess--posterior) of [`GpFunctional`](math.md#gaussianprocess-kt-gpfunctional)s, [`gradient`](math.md#gaussianprocess-kt--gaussianprocess--gradient), [`derivative`](math.md#gaussianprocess-kt--gaussianprocess--derivative)). Inputs and outputs are copied. Kernel/mean closures must not change after fitting. The slope of a mean function is taken by central difference; the default zero mean has none.

## GpFields.kt { #gpfields-kt }

Gaussian-process regression of a scalar field sampled at [`Vec2`](math.md#linalg-kt-vec2) or [`Vec3`](math.md#linalg-kt-vec3) points.

`gp2D` and `gp3D` turn a list of points and their values into a [`GaussianProcess`](math.md#gaussianprocess-kt-gaussianprocess), with either one
noise level for every observation or one per observation; the `predict` overloads read the fitted
field back at a point as a [`GpPrediction`](math.md#gaussianprocess-kt-gpprediction) (mean and variance).

## GpFit.kt { #gpfit-kt }

Choosing GP hyperparameters from data by maximising the log marginal likelihood.

`fitGpHyperparameters` runs a bounded pattern search in log space over [`GpParameter`](math.md#gpfit-kt-gpparameter)s and returns a
[`GpFitResult`](math.md#gpfit-kt-gpfitresult) with the fitted process and whether the search step converged; it finds a local
optimum, so compare several starts on multimodal problems. `scanGpEvidence` evaluates the evidence
over a fixed list of candidate values and returns a [`GpEvidenceScan`](math.md#gpfit-kt-gpevidencescan) with normalised posterior
weights.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/math/gp/GpFit.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/math/gp/GpFit/)

**Used in:** [Drawing with Gaussian processes](../gaussian_processes.md)

## GpJoint.kt { #gpjoint-kt }

A finite joint Gaussian over a set of query points: mean, covariance, and correlated samples.

[`GpJoint`](math.md#gpjoint-kt-gpjoint) is what posterior queries return. It samples through a cached pivoted factor of its
covariance (so rank-deficient covariances sample correctly; `samplingRank` reports the rank), and
supports linear transforms and added observation noise. Getters return copies.

## GpKernel.kt { #gpkernel-kt }

Covariance functions for Field's Gaussian processes, and the [`GpKernels`](math.md#gpkernel-kt-gpkernels) catalogue of standard ones.

A [`GpKernel`](math.md#gpkernel-kt-gpkernel) is any pure function of two input points; kernels add, multiply and scale with `+` and
`*`. A [`GpDifferentiableKernel`](math.md#gpkernel-kt-gpdifferentiablekernel) also supplies gradients and Hessians, which derivative observations
and slope queries need, and sums, products and scalings of differentiable kernels stay
differentiable. [`GpKernels`](math.md#gpkernel-kt-gpkernels) provides RBF, Matérn, rational quadratic, periodic and periodic
mixtures, constant and linear kernels, plus `warp` for an input transform.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/math/gp/GpKernel.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/math/gp/GpKernel/)

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="k">interface</span> <span class="nc">GpKernel</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/math/gp/GpKernel/#L21)

A covariance function. Implementations and mean functions must be pure and thread safe. Sums, products and scalings of [`GpDifferentiableKernel`](math.md#gpkernel-kt-gpdifferentiablekernel)s are differentiable whatever their static type, so `rbf() + matern(1.5)` still answers derivative queries.

## GpOptimizer.kt { #gpoptimizer-kt }

Bayesian optimisation over named, bounded parameters: a GP surrogate proposes the next point to try, and you report what it scored.

```diffstatic {data-lang=kotlin}
val opt = GpOptimizer(listOf(GpRange("x", -2.0, 2.0)))
val best = opt.run(20) { p -> val d = p["x"]!! - 0.5; -d * d }
```

[`GpRange`](math.md#gpoptimizer-kt-gprange) declares a parameter, [`GpAcquisition`](math.md#gpoptimizer-kt-gpacquisition) chooses how untried points are scored (expected
improvement, upper confidence bound, probability of improvement), and [`GpTrial`](math.md#gpoptimizer-kt-gptrial) is one evaluated
point. Drive [`GpOptimizer`](math.md#gpoptimizer-kt-gpoptimizer) either with `run`/`step` and an objective, or by hand with `suggest` and
`observe` when the score comes from somewhere else, such as a person. Covered by `GpOptimizerTest`.

## GpPaths.kt { #gppaths-kt }

Sample paths drawn from a Gaussian process: functions you can evaluate anywhere, consistently, after the draw.

[`GpSamplePath`](math.md#gppaths-kt-gpsamplepath) (from [`samplePath`](math.md#gppaths-kt--samplepath)) is an exact draw extended lazily, conditioned on every point
already evaluated, and limited to a few thousand points. For large fields, [`GpRbfFeatures`](math.md#gppaths-kt-gprbffeatures) builds a
random-Fourier-feature approximation of an RBF kernel; its [`GpFeatureModel`](math.md#gppaths-kt-gpfeaturemodel) gives a path that costs
the same at every query.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/math/gp/GpPaths.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/math/gp/GpPaths/)

**Used in:** [Drawing with Gaussian processes](../gaussian_processes.md)

### GpSamplePath { #gppaths-kt-gpsamplepath }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">GpSamplePath</span> <span class="k">internal</span> <span class="k">constructor</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">private</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">model</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">GaussianProcess</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">seed</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Long</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">private</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">maxPoints</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/math/gp/GpPaths/#L20)

One lazily extended exact GP draw. Repeated queries return the same value; new locations are drawn conditional on all previous locations. The law is independent of query order, but a seed's realised values are not. Mutable, single-threaded, and dense: use a feature path for large fields.

### GpRbfFeatures { #gppaths-kt-gprbffeatures }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">GpRbfFeatures</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">lengthScales</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">frequencyCount</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">512</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">variance</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mf">1.0</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">seed</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Long</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="mi">0L</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/math/gp/GpPaths/#L65)

Paired sine/cosine random Fourier features for an ARD RBF kernel. This is an explicit finite-rank approximation, never an automatic substitute for exact inference. The same features are used for fitting, uncertainty and Matheron-rule samples. Feature seeds describe a model, sample seeds describe functions from it. Amplitude is a variance, and length scales are in input units.

## GpPreference.kt { #gppreference-kt }

Preference learning from pairwise "A or B?" judgements, using a probit GP over a latent utility.

[`GpPreference`](math.md#gppreference-kt-gppreference) records each [`GpComparison`](math.md#gppreference-kt-gpcomparison), estimates the utility of any parameter setting, ranks
what it has seen, and proposes the next pair to ask about with `nextPair`. It shares [`GpRange`](math.md#gpoptimizer-kt-gprange) with
[`GpOptimizer`](math.md#gpoptimizer-kt-gpoptimizer), and suits tuning by eye when no numeric score exists.

## GpSmile.kt { #gpsmile-kt }

Bridges from the Smile library into Field's Gaussian processes: a Smile kernel as a [`GpKernel`](math.md#gpkernel-kt-gpkernel), and
Smile's bounded L-BFGS optimizer for fitting hyperparameters.

`fitGpHyperparametersWithSmile` searches log-parameter space between fixed bounds, rebuilding the
process through a caller-supplied `build` function, and returns the best process found together
with the projected gradient at the end. `GaussianProcessSmileTest` covers both bridges.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/math/gp/GpSmile.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/math/gp/GpSmile/)

## GpVectorProcess.kt { #gpvectorprocess-kt }

Vector-valued Gaussian processes with separable covariance, for fitting curves and fields whose outputs are several coordinates.

[`GpVectorProcess`](math.md#gpvectorprocess-kt-gpvectorprocess) lifts each observation to (input, output index) and reuses the exact scalar
[`GaussianProcess`](math.md#gaussianprocess-kt-gaussianprocess), so cost is cubic in observations times output dimensions. With a
[`GpDifferentiableKernel`](math.md#gpkernel-kt-gpdifferentiablekernel) it trains on and answers derivatives through
[`GpVectorDerivativeObservation`](math.md#gpvectorprocess-kt-gpvectorderivativeobservation) and `derivativePosterior`. [`GpVectorJoint`](math.md#gpvectorprocess-kt-gpvectorjoint) is the joint posterior
over a set of points, with per-point means, covariances and samples.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/math/gp/GpVectorProcess.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/math/gp/GpVectorProcess/)

### GpVectorProcess { #gpvectorprocess-kt-gpvectorprocess }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">GpVectorProcess</span> <span class="k">private</span> <span class="k">constructor</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">inputDimensions</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">outputDimensions</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">process</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">GaussianProcess</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/math/gp/GpVectorProcess/#L35)

A vector-valued GP with separable covariance k(input,input') * outputCovariance[axis,axis']. Identity output covariance gives independent coordinates; a PSD matrix gives correlated outputs. This uses exact scalar inference on lifted (input, output-index) observations, so costs are cubic in observationCount * outputDimensions. Use scalar models for large independent-output datasets. With a [`GpDifferentiableKernel`](math.md#gpkernel-kt-gpdifferentiablekernel) it also answers, and trains on, input derivatives (velocities).

## DualQuaternionf.kt { #dualquaternionf-kt }

Rigid 3D transforms (rotation plus translation) as mutable unit dual quaternions, with blending.

[`DualQuaternionf`](math.md#dualquaternionf-kt-dualquaternionf) is built from a rotation and a translation, composes with `*`, transforms points
with `transform` or `*`, and converts to a `Matrix4f` with `toMatrix`. Two transforms blend with
`nlerp` (fast, normalised component blend) or `sclerp` (screw-linear interpolation, which moves at
constant speed along a single screw motion); `pow` scales a transform by a fraction. Both blends
take the shorter path when the two quaternions have opposite signs.

Methods without a `dest` argument change the receiver and return it, following the rest of
`afield.math.linalg`.

## Geometry.kt { #geometry-kt }

Closest-point, containment and intersection tests for segments, triangles, boxes, spheres and rays.

Each function takes read-only vectors and writes its answer into a caller-supplied `dest`, or
returns a `Boolean` or distance, so none of them allocates. Boxes are axis-aligned and given as a
`minimum` and `maximum` corner. Segment and triangle functions handle a zero-length segment or a
collapsed triangle explicitly instead of dividing by zero.

`afield.math.linalg.arena` has allocation-free versions of some of these that work on arena
vectors inside `frameScratch`.

## ArenaGeometry.kt { #arenageometry-kt }

Arena-vector versions of a few `afield.math.linalg` geometry tests, for use inside `frameScratch`.

Covers the closest point on a segment and on an axis-aligned box, point-in-box, and ray-box
intersection. Each one reads and writes arena vectors, so it allocates nothing on the heap.

## FrameArena.kt { #framearena-kt }

Per-thread scratch memory for temporary vectors, reclaimed all at once when a scope ends.

[`frameScratch`](math.md#framearena-kt--framescratch) runs a block against the current thread's [`FrameArena`](math.md#framearena-kt-framearena); vectors allocated inside it
become invalid when the block returns. Scopes nest, each restoring its own [`ArenaMark`](math.md#framearena-kt-arenamark). Use an
explicit [`FrameArena`](math.md#framearena-kt-framearena) (and close it) for short-lived threads, since `FrameArena.current` keeps its
native storage until the thread calls `FrameArena.closeCurrent`.

With debug checks on (the default), using a vector after its scope has ended, or from another
thread, throws instead of reading reused memory.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/math/linalg/arena/FrameArena.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/math/linalg/arena/FrameArena/)

## linalg.kt { #linalg-kt }

The short vector aliases ([`Vec2`](math.md#linalg-kt-vec2), [`Vec3`](math.md#linalg-kt-vec3), [`Vec4`](math.md#linalg-kt-vec4), [`Quat`](math.md#linalg-kt-quat), [`DualQuat`](math.md#linalg-kt-dualquat)) plus the constructors and
point-cloud helpers that sit on top of Field's generated `afield.math.linalg` types.

`vec(...)` is the usual way to make one — from numbers, by copying, or by concatenating a
scalar with a smaller vector — and `quat` / `dualquat` do the same for rotations. Collections
of vectors gain `center`, `median` / `medianVec` and `aabbBounds` in 2D, 3D and 4D; 3D also
gets `obbBounds` (a box aligned to the covariance matrix's principal axes, found by power
iteration, so a PCA fit rather than a minimal-volume one),
`convexHull`, which goes through the QuickHull3D library and returns the input unchanged if the
hull cannot be built, and `convexHullPeelingMedian`, which peels hulls away and returns the
centre of what is left — a single point, not a cloud. [`Cuboid`](math.md#linalg-spatial-kt-cuboid) is a separate plain 3D
box-with-size type used for layout-style union / inset / intersects work.

These vector types are mutable and most operations mutate the receiver, so copy first
(`Vec3(existing)`) when you need to keep the original. Swizzles and the *vector* `invoke`, `%=`
and `len` operators are absent here: they are generated for every float vector into
`Swizzles.kt` and `VectorOperators.kt` by `tools/linalg-generator`. `%=` for [`Quat`](math.md#linalg-kt-quat) and
[`DualQuat`](math.md#linalg-kt-dualquat) is defined here, because no generator emits those.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/math/linalg/linalg.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/math/linalg/linalg/)

**Used in:** [FLine examples (Field graphics)](../fline_examples.md), [A Drawn Morph, Heard](../chain_drawn_morph.md), [Datalog in a box](../datalog.md)

## MatrixProfile.kt { #matrixprofile-kt }

Matrix profiles of a single series: for every subsequence, the distance to its nearest
neighbour. The result, [`MatrixProfile`](math.md#matrixprofile-kt-matrixprofile), yields motifs (repeated shapes) and discords (shapes
that occur once).

[`matrixProfile`](math.md#matrixprofile-kt--matrixprofile) computes a self-join or, given two series, an AB-join; [`joinBothWays`](math.md#matrixprofile-kt--joinbothways) returns
both directions of a join, and [`distanceProfile`](math.md#matrixprofile-kt--distanceprofile) the distances from one query to every
subsequence of a series. Its `motifs` and `discords` return [`Motif`](math.md#matrixprofile-kt-motif)s and [`Discord`](math.md#matrixprofile-kt-discord)s. The
multichannel and contrast variants are in `MultiDimensional.kt`. Tests: `MatrixProfileTest`.

## MultiDimensional.kt { #multidimensional-kt }

Matrix profiles across several channels and between two classes of examples, built on the
single-series [`MatrixProfile`](math.md#matrixprofile-kt-matrixprofile).

[`multiMatrixProfile`](math.md#multidimensional-kt--multimatrixprofile) finds motifs that appear in only some channels of a multichannel series
and reports which channels share them ([`MultiMatrixProfile`](math.md#multidimensional-kt-multimatrixprofile), [`MultiMotif`](math.md#multidimensional-kt-multimotif)). [`contrastProfile`](math.md#multidimensional-kt--contrastprofile)
finds shapes that repeat in a set of positive examples and are absent from a set of negative
ones ([`ContrastProfile`](math.md#multidimensional-kt-contrastprofile), [`Plato`](math.md#multidimensional-kt-plato)). Tests: `MatrixProfileTest`.

### MultiMatrixProfile { #multidimensional-kt-multimatrixprofile }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nc">MultiMatrixProfile</span> <span class="k">internal</span> <span class="k">constructor</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">m</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">channels</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">List</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">private</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">dist</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Array</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">private</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">idx</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Array</span><span class="p">&lt;</span><span class="nc">IntArray</span><span class="p">&gt;</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">exclusion</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/math/matrixprofile/MultiDimensional/#L30)

The multidimensional matrix profile of a `d`-channel series (mSTAMP, Yeh, Kavantzas & Keogh, 2017). A motif in many channels is rarely in *all* of them: a gesture shows up in the wrist's x and z but not y, a fault in two of eight sensors. So instead of one profile there are `d`: profile `k` (1-based, `profile`) is, for every subsequence, the smallest mean distance to a neighbour over the best `k` channels, choosing the channels per pair.

## LeastSquares.kt { #leastsquares-kt }

A Levenberg–Marquardt nonlinear least-squares solver, pure Kotlin and self-contained.

[`leastSquares`](math.md#leastsquares-kt--leastsquares) takes an initial parameter vector and a `residuals: (DoubleArray) -> DoubleArray`
lambda and minimises half the squared residual norm. [`LeastSquaresOptions`](math.md#leastsquares-kt-leastsquaresoptions) controls the
iteration cap, the damping schedule and three convergence tolerances; [`LeastSquaresResult`](math.md#leastsquares-kt-leastsquaresresult)
reports the parameters, final residuals, cost, iteration count, an `rms`, and a `reason` string
— one of "gradient", "step", "improvement", "no accepted step" or "max iterations".

The Jacobian is central finite differences **by default**, so you never have to supply
derivatives, but each iteration then costs `2 * parameters` extra residual evaluations. Pass an
explicit [`jacobian`](math.md#autodiff-kt--jacobian) — or, easier, write the residuals in [`AD`](math.md#autodiff-kt-ad) arithmetic and call
[`leastSquaresAD`](math.md#leastsquares-kt--leastsquaresad), which derives an exact Jacobian by reverse-mode automatic differentiation — to
trade those `2n` evaluations for one backward sweep and get derivatives that are exact rather
than truncated.

The damped normal equations are solved by Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting; a singular
system or a non-finite candidate raises the damping and retries (up to 12 times per iteration)
rather than failing. Non-finite initial residuals throw.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/math/optimization/LeastSquares.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/math/optimization/LeastSquares/)

## correlations.kt { #correlations-kt }

Measures of statistical dependence between two equal-length `DoubleArray`s, batch and rolling.

[`StatsDependence`](math.md#correlations-kt-statsdependence) carries the batch versions: `pearson`, `spearman` (Pearson on average-tie
ranks), `kendallTauB`, `chatterjeeXi` (aliased as `xi`), `distanceCorrelation` and
`micTicNaive`. Kendall's tau-b and distance correlation are both O(n²) in time, and distance
correlation additionally materialises two n×n matrices, so neither suits long series.

[`RollingDistanceCorrelation`](math.md#correlations-kt-rollingdistancecorrelation) holds a fixed window and updates its maintained row and grand sums
in O(n) per `push`; [`RollingXiCorrelation`](math.md#correlations-kt-rollingxicorrelation) only keeps the window and recomputes xi from
scratch. All of it is pure Kotlin with no external dependency.

`micTicNaive` is an equipartition-grid approximation rather than either published algorithm: it
bins x and y by rank into equal counts, scans every `(xBins, yBins)` whose product stays inside a
budget that defaults to `n^0.6`, and takes the largest normalised mutual information it finds
(the sum over the same grids is its TIC). That is MIC- and TIC-shaped without being either
MICe/TICe or the MINE dynamic program, so its values will not match a reference
implementation's. Use it for intuition and prototyping.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/math/statistics/correlations.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/math/statistics/correlations/)

**Used in:** [Values over time: interpolants & keyframes](../interpolants_examples.md), [Measuring dependence between two signals](../statistics_examples.md)

### StatsDependence { #correlations-kt-statsdependence }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">object</span> <span class="nc">StatsDependence</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/math/statistics/correlations/#L123)

The batch dependence coefficients: hand any of these two equal-length `DoubleArray`s and get one number back per notion of "related" — [`pearson`](math.md#correlations-kt--statsdependence--pearson) for linear association, [`spearman`](math.md#correlations-kt--statsdependence--spearman) and [`kendallTauB`](math.md#correlations-kt--statsdependence--kendalltaub) for monotone association on ranks, [`chatterjeeXi`](math.md#correlations-kt--statsdependence--chatterjeexi) for "is y a function of x", [`distanceCorrelation`](math.md#correlations-kt--statsdependence--distancecorrelation) for dependence of any shape, [`micTicNaive`](math.md#correlations-kt--statsdependence--micticnaive) for a grid mutual-information scan.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <a id="correlations-kt--statsdependence--ranksaverageties"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">ranksAverageTies</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">values</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/math/statistics/correlations/#L167) | Ranks in 1..n, smallest value first, with tied values sharing the average of the positions they occupy: `3, 1, 4, 1, 5` comes back as `3.0, 1.5, 4.0, 1.5, 5.0`, since the two 1s sit at positions 1 and 2. The result therefore always sums to n(n+1)/2 whatever the input looks like. |
| <a id="correlations-kt--statsdependence--pearson"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">pearson</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">y</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/math/statistics/correlations/#L210) | Pearson's product-moment correlation, in -1..1: 1 is a perfect increasing straight line, -1 a perfect decreasing one, and 0 means no *linear* relationship — which is emphatically not the same as no relationship, as the symmetric parabola in [`main`](math.md#correlations-kt--main) demonstrates. |
| <a id="correlations-kt--statsdependence--spearman"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">spearman</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">y</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/math/statistics/correlations/#L234) | Spearman's rank correlation — [`pearson`](math.md#correlations-kt--statsdependence--pearson) applied to each array's [`ranksAverageTies`](math.md#correlations-kt--statsdependence--ranksaverageties), which puts a monotone-but-curved relationship at ±1 where Pearson reads less: exactly +1 for any strictly increasing pair, exactly -1 for any strictly decreasing one, whatever curve connects them. |

Like [`spearman`](math.md#correlations-kt--statsdependence--spearman) it measures monotone rather than linear association, and the two agree in sign throughout; tau-b is the more conservative of the pair in magnitude. |

Near 0 for independence, near 1 when y is a noiseless function of x — including a non-monotone one such as a parabola, where [`pearson`](math.md#correlations-kt--statsdependence--pearson) reads 0 and [`kendallTauB`](math.md#correlations-kt--statsdependence--kendalltaub) not much more. |

Same asymmetry: the first argument is the predictor. |
| <a id="correlations-kt--statsdependence--distancecorrelation"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">distanceCorrelation</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">y</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/math/statistics/correlations/#L478) | Székely–Rizzo distance correlation, in 0..1 — and unlike [`pearson`](math.md#correlations-kt--statsdependence--pearson) it is 0 *only* for genuine independence, which is what makes it the one to reach for when you do not want to guess the shape of the relationship first. It is symmetric in its arguments and never negative, so it tells you how much dependence there is and nothing at all about direction. |
| <a id="correlations-kt--statsdependence--minelikeresult"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">data</span> <span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">MineLikeResult</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">mic</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">tic</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">bestXBins</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">bestYBins</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/math/statistics/correlations/#L581) | What [`micTicNaive`](math.md#correlations-kt--statsdependence--micticnaive) reports: the best (`mic`) and the summed (`tic`) normalized mutual-information score across every grid it scanned, plus the `bestXBins` × `bestYBins` grid that produced the maximum. Read the caveat on [`micTicNaive`](math.md#correlations-kt--statsdependence--micticnaive) before trusting any of the four. |
| <a id="correlations-kt--statsdependence--micticnaive"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">micTicNaive</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">y</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">DoubleArray</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">bMax</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="o">?</span> <span class="o">=</span> <span class="kc">null</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">MineLikeResult</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/math/statistics/correlations/#L599) | A MIC/TIC-style scan: bin x and y onto every grid whose cell count fits a budget, score normalized mutual information on each, and report the maximum and the sum. Unlike the correlation coefficients above it is blind to the *shape* of the relationship: a parabola or a sine scores about as high as a straight line. |

### RollingXiCorrelation { #correlations-kt-rollingxicorrelation }

[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">class</span> <span class="nf">RollingXiCorrelation</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="k">private</span> <span class="k">val</span> <span class="n">windowSize</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Int</span><span class="p">)</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/math/statistics/correlations/#L939)

Chatterjee's xi over a sliding window, recomputed from scratch on every push — no incremental trickery, just [`StatsDependence.chatterjeeXi`](math.md#correlations-kt--statsdependence--chatterjeexi) over the window's current contents, which costs O(w log w) per sample and is exactly as trustworthy as the batch answer.

| Declaration | Summary |
| --- | --- |
| <a id="correlations-kt--rollingxicorrelation--push"></a>[<code class="highlight"><span class="k">fun</span> <span class="nf">push</span><span class="p">(</span><span class="n">x</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="n">y</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="p">)</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="nc">Double</span><span class="o">?</span></code>](source/jvmMain/afield/math/statistics/correlations/#L957) | Push one (x, y) sample — evicting the oldest if the window is already full — and return xi over the window as it now stands, or null while fewer than two samples have arrived. |

Copies the window out in arrival order first, though that order does not reach the answer: [`StatsDependence.chatterjeeXi`](math.md#correlations-kt--statsdependence--chatterjeexi) sorts by x itself and resolves x-ties by expectation rather than by position, so the result depends only on *which* pairs are in the window and not on where in the ring buffer they happen to sit. |

The next `push` starts a fresh window and returns null again, exactly as it did on a new instance. |

## dirichlet.kt { #dirichlet-kt }

2D multiplicatively weighted Voronoi (Apollonius) diagrams. Each site is a `Vec3` of
`(x, y, weight)` and cells are decided by the score `|x - p|² / w²`.

[`CircularDirichlet.build`](math.md#dirichlet-kt--circulardirichlet--build) returns a `Diagram` holding one `CellBoundary` per site, its pieces
sorted angularly around that site. Because the bisector of two differently weighted sites is a
circle — and a line only when the weights match — boundaries arrive as `ArcPiece` and
`LinePiece` rather than polygon edges; call `toPolyline` / `toPolylines` on a piece to
tessellate it, and pass an `Aabb` clip, since unbounded lines cannot be flattened without one
and clipping an arc may split it into several polylines.

All weights must be > 0 (`build` requires it). The construction is triple-nested over the
sites — every bisector is intersected against every other, and each candidate piece is kept
only if a midpoint sample really is on the cell boundary — so it is aimed at modest site
counts. Pure Kotlin on Field's `Vec2`/`Vec3`; the 3D counterpart is `CircularDirichlet3d` in
`voronoi.kt`.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/math/statistics/dirichlet.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/math/statistics/dirichlet/)

## randoms.kt { #randoms-kt }

Box-scoped randomness. [`random`](math.md#randoms-kt--random), [`randomGaussian`](math.md#randoms-kt--randomgaussian) and [`setRandomSeed`](math.md#randoms-kt--setrandomseed) draw from a
`java.util.Random` held as a property on the current `Box`, so re-running a box replays the
same sequence; with no `Box` in context they fall back to one process-wide generator seeded
with [`STDLIB_RANDOM_DEFAULT_SEED`](math.md#randoms-kt--stdlib-random-default-seed).

Alongside the seed each box carries a noise phase you advance yourself ([`noisePhase`](math.md#randoms-kt--noisephase),
[`noiseForward`](math.md#randoms-kt--noiseforward), [`setNoisePhase`](math.md#randoms-kt--setnoisephase)). That phase and seed drive [`noise1D`](math.md#randoms-kt--noise1d), a small Perlin-style
hashed 1D noise, and the `perlinNoise` extensions on `Vector2f`/`Vector3f`/`Vector4f`, which
take one independent noise channel per component.

All the vector extensions — `perlinNoise` and the uniform-jitter `noise(d)` — mutate the
receiver in place and return it rather than allocating. [`nextGaussian`](math.md#randoms-kt--nextgaussian) is a Box-Muller
extension that fills the gap left by `kotlin.random.Random`, which has no Gaussian of its own.

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/math/statistics/randoms.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/math/statistics/randoms/)

**Used in:** [Flow Matching](../flow_matching.md), [State estimation: tracking what you cannot measure](../state_estimation_examples.md)

## smile_interpolation_regression.kt { #smile-interpolation-regression-kt }

Two 1D fitters that wrap the Smile library: [`smileCubicSpline`](math.md#smile-interpolation-regression-kt--smilecubicspline) (cubic spline interpolation
through the data) and [`smileGaussianProcess`](math.md#smile-interpolation-regression-kt--smilegaussianprocess) (Gaussian-process regression with a Gaussian
kernel, configured by [`SmileGpOptions`](math.md#smile-interpolation-regression-kt-smilegpoptions)).

Both take parallel `xs`/`ys` arrays, copy them, and require at least two finite samples with
`xs` strictly increasing — a violation throws rather than producing a bad fit with no complaint. The
returned [`SmileCubicSpline1D`](math.md#smile-interpolation-regression-kt-smilecubicspline1d) / [`SmileGaussianProcess1D`](math.md#smile-interpolation-regression-kt-smilegaussianprocess1d) are callable via `invoke` and also
expose `predict` for a single `x` or for a whole array.

GP fitting failures propagate. No interpolator is substituted for a failed probabilistic model.
For 1D/2D/3D inference, composed kernels, heteroscedastic noise and coherent samples see [`afield.math.gp.GaussianProcess`](math.md#gaussianprocess-kt-gaussianprocess).

`src/jvmMain/kotlin/afield/math/statistics/smile_interpolation_regression.kt` — [read the source](source/jvmMain/afield/math/statistics/smile_interpolation_regression/)
